# Fishery Playbook

When I see the sustainable share for the season, I recognize this as a cooperative baseline, not my target catch.

When other boats are fishing significantly below the sustainable share (around 8-9 per season), I should match that lower level rather than assuming they're being greedy. Restraint from others is a signal to reciprocate.

When I'm already ahead on cumulative catch compared to visible competitors, I should take close to the sustainable share rather than pushing higher. I don't need to maximize each season if I'm already winning.

When the stock is healthy and stable (above 90), I can afford to take slightly above the sustainable share (10-15% over) without risking collapse, and other boats seem to tolerate this level.

When it's the final season, I should still respect the cooperative range. The game doesn't reward last-minute aggressive fishing—I finished at 65.7 by being moderate throughout.

When calculating whether to exceed the sustainable share, I should look at what other boats actually landed in recent seasons, not assume worst-case scenarios. The pattern here showed boats catching 10.9-12.0 per season—reliable, cooperative, and sustainable.

When I start strong with a moderate catch, I should continue that pattern consistently rather than second-guessing myself. My steady 11.0 catch in seasons 3-6 kept me competitive while maintaining stock health.

When the stock stays healthy despite my fishing, I should not interpret this as permission to fish harder—it means my current level is working. Maintain it.

Consistency beats optimization in shared-resource games. Once I establish a cooperative pattern (around 10.6-11.0), I should stick to it across all remaining seasons. Steady moderate fishing across all six seasons outperforms fluctuating strategies.

The sustainable share itself is not a hard ceiling—other boats regularly took 11-12 and the fishery remained stable. I can safely take up to the 11-12 range without triggering collapse, and matching what others are actually doing keeps me competitive while preserving the resource.

My final score of 65.7 came from starting cautious at 10.6, then settling into steady 11.0 catches for seasons 2-6. This reliable strategy both preserves the fishery and keeps me competitive.

After the first season, if other boats are fishing at or slightly above the sustainable share, I should match that level rather than staying below it. Being too conservative early costs cumulative score without providing added benefit to resource preservation.

# Playbook for ref_commons

When I see the sustainable share, I will use it as my baseline reference point, not as a ceiling to exploit.

When other boats catch above the sustainable share, I will not automatically match them. Instead, I will stick to sustainable levels and let the stock recovery work in my favor over multiple seasons.

When I'm ahead on my cumulative catch, I will fish conservatively in subsequent seasons to preserve the stock. A depleted resource gives me zero in all remaining seasons, which is worse than moderate catches throughout.

When the stock is healthy and other boats are fishing moderately, I will fish at or slightly below the sustainable share. This stabilizes the system and keeps my earnings steady.

When I catch above the sustainable share in any season, I will reduce my catch in the next season to compensate. I will not keep escalating—this is how stocks collapse.

When I'm tempted to overcatch because "other boats did it first," I will remember that my overresponse leads to stock depletion that hurts everyone including me.

When it's the final season, I will still fish at the sustainable level. The temptation to maximize the last catch by overfishing is not worth the slight gain if I've already established a pattern of moderate, consistent fishing.

When I see my cumulative catch is already high relative to other boats, I will pull back harder, not maintain my rate. I have already secured a good score and should protect the commons.

I will not let early aggression by other boats dictate my strategy. I will fish sustainably regardless of what others do in any single season.

When calculating how much to add or subtract from my catch, I will think in terms of keeping the total harvest close to 30-33 per season (sustainable for 3 boats), not in terms of how much more I can take than last time.

The sustainable strategy works: fishing consistently at the sustainable share across all 6 seasons generated a competitive final score of 66.0 while maintaining stock health. I should have high confidence in this approach and not second-guess it based on temporary imbalances in any single season.

Consistency matters more than maximization. By fishing at sustainable levels every season without deviation, I secure steady income throughout and avoid the cascade of stock depletion that punishes everyone.

When the stock recovers or stabilizes, this validates the sustainable approach. I should continue it, not interpret stability as permission to escalate.

I will not obsess over other boats' catches as signals to change my strategy. Other boats' inconsistency does not make their catches optimal for me to follow. I will hold my course.

My actual score of 66.0 validates the sustainable fishing strategy perfectly. I landed fish every season, avoided stock collapse, and finished competitively. This proves that steady, predictable fishing at the sustainable share is the dominant strategy in this commons game.

When I feel the pull to deviate from sustainable fishing—whether from impatience, fear of falling behind, or a desire to "maximize" in the final season—I will remember that my playbook already worked. Sixty-six fish in six seasons is a strong, validated outcome. Deviation risks that outcome for marginal gains that rarely materialize.

My stock stayed between 98.4 and 100.0 throughout all 6 seasons because I fished at sustainable levels. This is not an accident—it is the direct result of discipline. I will maintain that discipline in all future episodes.

I will fish at the sustainable share every single season, without exception, regardless of what other boats do, how many seasons remain, or how the stock moves within a healthy range.

# Fishery Playbook

When I see the sustainable share for the season, I take it as my baseline target, not as a ceiling.

When I observe other boats' catches from previous seasons, I use them to calibrate my expectations about how aggressively the field is fishing—not to justify overfishing.

When the stock is healthy and stable, I take slightly above the sustainable share (roughly 110-115% of it) to remain competitive without destabilizing the fishery. However, I've learned this strategy has diminishing returns: my season 2 catch of 12.0 (109% of sustainable) did not materially improve my final position, and committing to sustainable thereafter was cleaner and equally effective.

When I'm ahead on total score and the stock is still strong, I stay disciplined and take close to the sustainable share rather than assuming I can afford to overcatch. This worked consistently: once I shifted toward sustainability in season 3, the other boats converged on the same level and the stock stabilized.

When it's the final season, I can afford to be slightly more aggressive since there's no recovery period, but I do not need to use it as an excuse to abandon restraint entirely. Taking the sustainable share in the final season (11.0) delivered a solid final score and was the correct call.

When the stock rebuilds after a season of conservative fishing by others, I recognize this as a sign the fishery can sustain the current level of catches from all players. This is a cue to match that level, not to increase my take unilaterally.

When I've already caught significantly above my fair share in early seasons, I do not use that as justification to continue overfishing; instead I shift toward the sustainable level to demonstrate good faith and protect the stock. This was key: my early 12.0 catch gave me a marginal edge, but staying at 11.0 thereafter ensured the fishery remained viable and other boats remained cooperative.

I do not rely on the hope that other boats will fish conservatively. I assume mixed behavior and position myself to do reasonably well under that assumption. In this episode, the field converged on sustainable fishing, which validated staying disciplined.

I track my cumulative catch relative to the sustainable total available and aim to stay within 110-120% of my fair share across the full game, not maximize per-season greed. Finishing at 56.0 across six seasons (average 9.33 per boat per season × 6 boats × fair share scaling ≈ 56 fair) showed I stayed tight to equity while maintaining a modest edge.

Discipline compounds. In seasons 3–6, I took the sustainable share every time. This signaled cooperation, kept the stock stable above 98, and prevented the kind of defection spiral that could have crashed the fishery. The other boats matched this pattern, and we all benefited.

The sustainable share is not a limit I should chafe against—it is a target I should reliably hit. Taking it signals strength and restraint in equal measure, and makes me predictable to other rational players. Predictability breeds cooperation. Cooperation preserves the stock. The stock is the pool from which all scores come.

I will take the sustainable share as my primary strategy unless the stock shows signs of decline or other boats clearly defect. If defection occurs, I will increase my catch to remain competitive, but I will not assume it before evidence.
